title: Minimum Starting Vertices to Reach All Nodes
statement: You are given an integer n and a list of directed edges over nodes labeled 0 to n-1. Each edge [a, b] means there is a one-way path from a to b, and the edges are guaranteed to form a DAG (no cycles). Return the smallest possible set of starting nodes such that, beginning from those nodes and following edges forward, every node in the graph can be reached. Return the answer as a list of node labels sorted in ascending order. The unique smallest such set is exactly the set of nodes that have no incoming edge (in-degree zero): any node with an incoming edge is reachable from some other node, so it never needs to be a starting point, while a node with no incoming edge can only be reached by starting there. If n is 0, return an empty list.
hints: Instead of searching outward from every candidate node, ask which nodes could never be reached from anywhere else.
The key quantity is in-degree: a node is reachable from another node exactly when it has at least one incoming edge, so the answer is every node whose in-degree is zero.

Build an in-degree count by scanning each edge [a, b] and incrementing in_degree[b], then collect and return every node index in range(n) whose in-degree count stayed at zero, which range(n) already yields in ascending order.
